6.4 A Framework for Fund Due Diligence

This content was generated by AI. It may contain errors and is not investment advice.

All lessons, questions and reference answers on this site were generated by AI and have not been reviewed by a professional. Their correctness is not guaranteed. If you find an error, please report it with the link at the bottom of the page. The content is for learning only and is not investment advice.

What due diligence must answer

Section titled “What due diligence must answer”

Due diligence is a systematic check of a fund before investing in it (and while holding it), answering three questions: What is the fund doing? Has it consistently done what it says? What do investors pay for this, and what risks do they bear?

A common framework splits the check into several parts:

  1. Strategy: what the fund invests in, how it plans to make money, and why that approach should work.
  2. Process and people: who makes the decisions and how, whether the team and the firm are stable, and whether incentives are aligned with investors.
  3. Performance: where returns come from, and how they compare with a suitable benchmark and with similar funds.
  4. Costs and capacity: the total cost, and whether the strategy can still be carried out as the fund grows.
  5. Risk: how the fund could lose money, what the worst case is, and whether its liquidity can meet redemptions.

Morningstar’s fund ratings use people, process and parent (the fund company) as their main pillars, combined with fees, rather than relying directly on past returns.

Check C1
Due diligence frameworks put people and process first rather than choosing funds directly by past returns. The main reason is:
Returns over various periods are on every factsheet. The issue is not getting them but what they can tell us.
Can due diligence guarantee results? What can it do?

Strategy, process and people

Section titled “Strategy, process and people”

Checking the strategy means comparing what the fund says with what it does: whether the objective and strategy in the prospectus (6.3 Active vs. Passive Investing) match its actual holdings, turnover and risk statistics. A change in the style of the holdings over time, for example a “value fund” gradually buying many growth stocks, is called style drift; it makes the fund’s role in a portfolio unpredictable.

On people, look at: the manager’s tenure, and whether the past record was produced by the current team; whether decisions depend on one person or a team (key-person risk); how much the managers have invested in the fund themselves, which the statement of additional information (SAI) discloses in ranges, the top one being “over 1 million dollars”; and whether the fund company is mainly an investment firm or mainly focused on sales and growing assets (principal-agent problem).

Check C2
A fund's manager has invested over 1 million dollars in the fund he runs. From this one can be sure the fund will beat its benchmark.
What does the manager investing his own money say about his interests and investors'? Does it guarantee his judgment is right?

Performance attribution

Section titled “Performance attribution”

Performance attribution splits a fund’s excess return over its benchmark into its sources. The common Brinson method splits it by sector (or region, or asset class): wiw_iwi​ and RiR_iRi​ are the fund’s weight and return in category iii, wiBw_i^BwiB​ and RiBR_i^BRiB​ the benchmark’s, and RBR^BRB is the benchmark’s total return.

A=∑i(wi−wiB)(RiB−RB)S=∑iwi(Ri−RiB)A = \sum_i \left(w_i - w_i^B\right)\left(R_i^B - R^B\right) \qquad S = \sum_i w_i \left(R_i - R_i^B\right)A=i∑​(wi​−wiB​)(RiB​−RB)S=i∑​wi​(Ri​−RiB​)

AAA is the allocation effect: the return from overweighting sectors that beat the benchmark as a whole and underweighting those that lagged. SSS is the selection effect: the return from picking securities within each sector that beat that sector’s benchmark. Their sum equals the fund’s total excess return R−RBR - R^BR−RB (Exercises Question 1).

Another method needs no holdings, only returns: regress the fund’s returns on factors such as market, size and value (4.6 Multifactor Models) to see which factor exposures explain the returns; only the remaining intercept is alpha. This is called returns-based style analysis.

Check C3
Under the default settings of Figure 3-1, the fund beats its benchmark by 0.5 percentage points. Which statement is correct?
Look at the two bars. Is the selection effect positive or negative? How does the fund's return in A compare with A's benchmark return of 20%?
The two effects sum to 0.5, but what are their individual sizes and signs? Look at the readout.

Size, capacity and costs

Section titled “Size, capacity and costs”

Fees and other costs (6.2 Fund Costs) are part of due diligence: what should be compared is the total cost and the return over the benchmark after all costs.

Another question is size. Many active strategies have limited capacity: as a fund grows, each trade gets larger and moves prices, raising market impact costs (turnover ratio), and there are fewer good opportunities available in sufficient size. The model of Berk and Green (2004) argues that if investors put money into funds with good past performance, money keeps flowing in until the fund is so large that its excess return is eaten up by costs. Some funds close to new investors when they become too large.

Check C4
An active small-cap fund has done very well over the past 5 years, and its assets grew from 500 million to 8 billion dollars, with the same strategy and managers. What investors should worry about most is:
As a fund grows, fixed costs are spread over more assets; does the expense ratio usually rise or fall?
How would that affect investment results? Think about how size affects carrying out a small-cap strategy.

Risk and liquidity

Section titled “Risk and liquidity”

Checking risk means more than looking at the standard deviation. Also look at: the maximum drawdown (maximum drawdown) and the market conditions in which it happened; concentration (top ten holdings, sectors); the use of leverage and derivatives; and the credit quality and liquidity of the assets held.

One especially important issue is liquidity mismatch: a fund lets investors redeem every day but holds assets that take a long time to sell at a reasonable price. In December 2015 the US Third Avenue Focused Credit Fund suspended redemptions because it held many hard-to-sell high-yield bonds; in June 2019 the UK’s Woodford Equity Income Fund also suspended redemptions, having held many unlisted and small-cap stocks.

Check C5
A fund with daily redemptions holds 30% hard-to-sell assets. As long as daily redemptions are normally small, this arrangement carries little risk.
If news triggers many redemptions, which assets does the fund sell first to pay? What are the remaining holders left with? What will investors who understand this do?

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • Due diligence answers: what the fund is doing, whether it consistently does what it says, and what investors pay and bear.
  • Compare the strategy with actual holdings and watch for style drift; look at the manager’s tenure, the team, the managers’ own investment and the firm’s incentives.
  • Performance attribution splits excess return into allocation and selection effects; returns-based style analysis uses factor regressions to separate factor exposures from alpha.
  • Compare total costs; active strategies have limited capacity, and excessive size erodes excess returns.
  • Risk includes drawdowns, concentration, leverage and liquidity; a fund with daily redemptions holding hard-to-sell assets has a liquidity mismatch.

Exercises

Section titled “Exercises”
Question 1
A fund and its benchmark have the following weights and returns in three sectors (weights as shares of the fund or benchmark). Technology: benchmark 30% with a 25% return, fund 50% with 20%; Health care: benchmark 20% with 5%, fund 20% with 8%; Energy: benchmark 50% with −5%, fund 30% with −4%.
(a) Show that in the Brinson decomposition the allocation and selection effects sum to R−RBR - R^BR−RB.
(b) Compute the allocation effect, selection effect and total excess return for the year.
(c) The manager says: "We beat our benchmark this year through excellent stock picking." Evaluate this statement, and say what you would check next.
Question 2
A US stock fund that describes itself as "deep research, selective stock picking" beat the S&P 500 by 3 percentage points a year on average over the past 5 years. Regressing its excess return (over the risk-free rate) on the market, size (SMB) and value (HML) factors gives: market 1.0, SMB 0.6, HML −0.3. Over these 5 years the SMB factor averaged 4% a year and HML −2% a year.
(a) Roughly how much of the yearly excess return do the factor exposures explain? What is alpha after removing them?
(b) Evaluate the claim that "selective stock picking produced 3 percentage points a year". What else in the regression should be checked?
Question 3
An analyst estimates that an active strategy can earn 2% a year above its benchmark before fees and market impact; market impact costs about 0.4% a year per 1 billion dollars of assets (proportional to assets). The expense ratio is 0.9% at 1 billion dollars of assets and falls to 0.7% at 8 billion.
(a) At 1 billion and at 8 billion dollars, roughly what is the investor's excess return after all costs?
(b) The fund company says: "As the fund grows its expense ratio has fallen, and the managers and strategy are unchanged, so this only benefits investors." Evaluate this statement. From the fund company's point of view, why might it still want the fund to keep growing?
Question 4
A fund with daily redemptions has 100 (million dollars) of assets: 70 that can be sold at NAV at any time, and 30 that are hard to sell; NAV values them at fair estimates, but if forced to sell quickly the fund gets only 80% of the estimate.
(a) A first group of investors redeems 20, paid from liquid assets. What share of the fund is then hard to sell? A second group redeems 40, also paid from liquid assets. If the remaining investors then need the fund to sell all its hard-to-sell assets under pressure, what percentage of their assets do they lose?
(b) The fund company says: "Our NAV reflects the fair value of the assets, so redeeming early or late makes no difference, and investors need not worry." Evaluate this statement. What can a fund do to reduce this problem?
